assumptions: The spaces \(\alpha,\beta\) carry arbitrary measurable structures, with the product measurable structure on \(\alpha\times\beta\).
The measure \(\gamma\) couples \(\mu\) and \(\nu\): its coordinate pushforwards satisfy \(\gamma.\mathrm{fst}=\mu\) and \(\gamma.\mathrm{snd}=\nu\).
Only \(\mu\) is assumed to be a probability measure. No finiteness or probability assumption on \(\gamma\) or \(\nu\) is supplied independently.

open MeasureTheory
namespace AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.Transport
def IsCoupling {α β : Type*} [MeasurableSpace α] [MeasurableSpace β]
    (γ : Measure (α × β)) (μ : Measure α) (ν : Measure β) : Prop :=
  γ.fst = μ ∧ γ.snd = ν
end AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.Transport
open AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.Transport
decoder_definitions: Measures take values in the nonnegative extended reals. IsProbabilityMeasure η is a Prop-valued typeclass asserting that η assigns mass one to the whole underlying space.
For a measure η on a product measurable space, η.fst and η.snd are its pushforwards under the first and second coordinate projections.
IsCoupling γ μ ν is the conjunction γ.fst=μ and γ.snd=ν, as defined in the given Lean context.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: Use the mass identity for a measurable coordinate pushforward and one prescribed probability marginal to recover the joint probability interface. This is one local measure-theoretic mechanism, not a code-length label.

The constructor tactic reduces IsProbabilityMeasure γ to its total-mass field. Rewriting by the reverse of Measure.fst_univ turns joint mass into first-marginal mass, hγ.1 substitutes μ, and measure_univ uses the existing probability instance for μ. The second conjunct hγ.2 is not needed. This is a fixed-target reconstruction, not a claim of finite moments or a solved transport problem.

mathematical_cores.question: Prove that γ is a probability measure by calculating its total mass from the coupling identities. Identify which marginal identity this argument uses and explain whether ν needs an additional probability assumption. Do not assume the desired joint normalization at the outset.

rubric.criterion: Reduces joint probability normalization to proving γ has total mass one, without assuming γ is already finite or a probability measure.
Uses the measurable first projection and its inverse image of the whole space to identify joint mass with first-marginal mass.
Uses γ.fst=μ and μ being a probability measure to obtain the exact mass one.
Identifies that the second-marginal identity is unused in this calculation and does not add a probability premise on ν.

It is not a quotation or completion of a textbook transport theorem. The family was already public before this QA was authored.
steps: Let \(\pi_1:\alpha\times\beta\to\alpha\) be the first projection, which is measurable for the product measurable structure. The inverse image of the whole first space is the whole product space: \[\pi_1^{-1}(\alpha)=\alpha\times\beta.\]

By the definition of pushforward mass and the prescribed first marginal, \[\gamma(\alpha\times\beta)=(\gamma.\mathrm{fst})(\alpha)=\mu(\alpha)=1.\] The last equality is exactly the probability assumption on μ.
A measure of total mass one is a probability measure. Thus γ has the required probability interface; its finiteness is a consequence, not an extra premise used to obtain the mass identity.

This deduction uses only the first marginal identity. The second marginal remains part of the coupling data but no separate probability assumption on ν is needed. This local mass result asserts no optimality, moment bound or integrability of arbitrary unbounded functions.
mathematical_cores.title: Recovering joint probability mass from one marginal

case-1.assumptions: μ is a probability measure, meaning μ assigns mass one to the whole space α. The hypothesis hγ asserts both γ.fst = μ and γ.snd = ν. The measurable-space structures are also assumed. There is no separate assumption that ν is a probability measure, and no separate probability, finiteness, or sigma-finiteness assumption on γ; the signature does not request independence or a product-measure representation.
case-1.conclusion: γ is a probability measure: γ assigns mass one to the whole space α × β. This is a Prop-valued assertion about the already quantified γ, not the construction or existence of a coupling. The stated conclusion does not separately assert that ν is a probability measure, uniqueness of γ, independence of the coordinates, or γ = μ.prod ν.
case-1.constants: The sole normalization constant is 1, the mass of the whole space required by IsProbabilityMeasure. There are no auxiliary constants, bounds, rates, thresholds, or dimension-dependent parameters in the proposition.
case-1.domains: α and β are arbitrary types, each equipped with a measurable space. γ is a measure on their product measurable space; μ and ν are measures on their respective factors. Measure values lie in the nonnegative extended reals. No topology, metric, countability, separability, or explicitly stated nonemptiness restriction is imposed on the types.
case-1.objects: Two underlying types α and β with measurable-space structures; measures μ on α and ν on β; a measure γ on α × β; and its coordinate pushforward measures γ.fst and γ.snd. IsCoupling γ μ ν names the conjunction of the two marginal equalities, not additional data or a selected construction of γ.
case-1.quantifiers: Universally quantified over arbitrary α and β, their measurable-space instances, and arbitrary measures γ : Measure (α × β), μ : Measure α, and ν : Measure β. The type and measure binders are implicit, and the measurable-space and IsProbabilityMeasure μ binders are typeclass arguments. Given any instance asserting that μ is a probability measure and any proof hγ of IsCoupling γ μ ν, the proposition IsProbabilityMeasure γ holds. There is no existential quantifier selecting a measure or coupling.
case-1.senses: The coupling conditions are exact equalities of measures, where the marginals are pushforwards under the coordinate projections. Probability means total mass exactly one in the nonnegative extended reals. The conclusion is not almost-everywhere equality, convergence, an asymptotic claim, an approximation, or an inequality. No additional properties are encoded by the locally supplied IsCoupling definition.
